text: Rached Ghannouchi (Arabic: راشد الغنوشي, romanized: Rāshid al-Ghannūshī; born 22 June 1941), also spelled Rachid al-Ghannouchi or Rached el-Ghannouchi, is a Tunisian politician and the co-founder of the Ennahdha Party, serving as its intellectual leader. He was born Rashad Khriji (راشد الخريجي) in El Hamma, in the governorate of Gabès in southern Tunisia, where his village had no electricity or paved roads. His father was a poor farmer, and the family worked in the fields daily, with meat only a few times a year; after the harvest, they wove baskets from palm leaves to supplement income. Rached attended a local branch of the traditional Arabic-language Zaytouna school with financial help from an older brother. He earned a certificate of attainment equivalent to the Baccalauréat in 1962 from the University of Ez-Zitouna (Zaytouna), then entered the school of agriculture at Cairo University in 1964 before leaving due to the expulsion of Tunisians from Egypt. He moved to Syria and studied philosophy at the University of Damascus, graduating in 1968. In his 20s, he traveled and worked in Europe as a grape picker and dish washer. In April 1981, Ghannouchi founded the Islamic Tendency Movement (Ḥarakat al-Ittijāh al-Islāmī), which described itself as rooted in non-violent Islamism and advocated for equitable economic life, the end of single-party politics, and political pluralism and democracy. By the end of July, he and his followers were arrested, sentenced to eleven years in prison in Bizerte, and tortured; both religious and secular communities, including secular political organizations, rallied in his support. While in prison, he translated works and wrote on democracy, women's rights, and Palestine, producing his most noted work, Al‐Hurriyat al‐'Ammah (Public Liberties). He was released in 1984, returned to prison in 1987 with a life sentence, and was released again in 1988. He moved to the United Kingdom as a political exile, living there for 22 years. In 1989, he attended the Islamic Committee for Palestine conference in Chicago. Following the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, he denounced King Fahd of Saudi Arabia for inviting U.S. forces and called for a Muslim boycott of American goods, planes, and ships. He has also been criticized for calling for jihad against Israel. He continued to criticize Tunisian politics and President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali. After Ben Ali was ousted in popular unrest, Ghannouchi returned to Tunisia on 30 January 2011, after twenty-two years in exile, welcomed by thousands. His party won 37.04% of the vote in the 2011 Tunisian Constituent Assembly election—more than the next four parties combined—and Ghannouchi did not take a government position; Hamadi Jebali became Prime Minister. Ennahda led Tunisia through the aftermath of the Jasmine Revolution, characterized by greater transparency, lack of corruption, and consensus-building. In March 2012, Ennahda declared it would not support making sharia the main source of legislation in the new constitution, maintaining the secular nature of the state, a stance criticized by hardline Islamists but welcomed by secular parties. The government faced criticism for mediocre economic performance, failure to stimulate tourism, poor relations with France, and tolerance of radical Islamists demanding Sharia law, gender equality, and restrictions on polygamy, some of whom were responsible for the September 2012 ransacking and burning of the American embassy and school following the assassinations of Chokri Belaid (February 2013) and Mohamed Brahmi (July 2013). During the 2013–14 Tunisian political crisis, secularists demanded the government step down or a Sisi-style coup, while Ennahda militants opposed early elections and booed Ghannouchi’s calls for national unity. Ghannouchi worked with secularist leader Beji Caid Essebsi to forge a compromise, signing a "road map" on October 5, 2013, whereby Ennahda would step down for a caretaker government after the new constitution was agreed upon and until new elections were held. Both leaders faced criticism from their party ranks, and Ghannouchi secured agreement from the Ennahda shura council only by threatening to resign. In January 2014, after the new Tunisian Constitution was approved, Ennahda peacefully quit government and handed power to a technocratic government led by Mehdi Jomaa. Ennahda placed second in the October 2014 parliamentary election with 27.79% of the vote and formed a coalition government with the larger secularist party Nidaa Tounes despite rank-and-file opposition. Ennahda did not put forth a presidential candidate in the November 2014 election; Ghannouchi "hinted broadly" that he personally supported Beji Caid Essebsi, who won with over 55% of the vote. Ghannouchi argued that the country was too fragile and the economy too in need of reform for Ennahda to remain in opposition. He supported a crackdown on jihadi indoctrination at radical mosques, as over 60 civilians, mostly tourists, were killed in 2015 by jihadis, severely damaging Tunisia’s tourism industry. Despite his Islamist background, he had always been "reviled" by jihadis and now appeared near the top of the jihadi "wanted list." On 22 October 2011, The Economist published an apology for previously attributing false statements to Ghannouchi, claiming he opposed the liberal Code of Personal Status and threatened to hang a Tunisian feminist, Raja bin Salama; the apology stated that Ghannouchi expressly accepted the Code of Personal Status and never threatened to hang bin Salama. On 9 October 2012, The Independent apologized for suggesting Ennahda had accepted foreign funds, clarifying that Ghannouchi and his party had not received any foreign donations in breach of Tunisian party funding laws. On 17 May 2013, the BBC apologized for previously accusing Ghannouchi of threatening to deploy troops if Ennahda did not achieve desired election results and suggesting he condoned the violent Salafist attack on the U.S. embassy and school in September 2012; the retraction acknowledged these claims were false and apologized for the distress caused. In 2020, the UK High Court ruled in Ghannouchi’s favor in a libel case against Middle East Online (MEO) and its editor Haitham El Zobaidi, who claimed Ennahda supported terrorism—a charge Ghannouchi "vigorously denied." According to Ahmed Yusuf, the article was part of a "systematic campaign" against Ghannouchi by media backed by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Egypt. On 1 February 2024, Ghannouchi and his son-in-law were sentenced to three years in prison by a Tunisian court for illicit foreign financing and ordered to pay a fine of $1.17 million on behalf of his party. On 19 February, he began a hunger strike in prison in solidarity with other opposition figures imprisoned by President Saied’s government. On 13 July 2024, his three-year sentence was confirmed by the Criminal Chamber of the Judicial and Financial Unit. On 8 July 2025, he was sentenced to 14 years’ imprisonment on terrorism charges. Ghannouchi’s willingness to compromise with secularists and Tunisia’s democratic success post-Arab Spring has been credited by at least one observer, Robert Worth, to his background—unlike many Islamists, he lived abroad for decades, reading widely in three languages, including Karl Marx, Sigmund Freud, and Jean-Paul Sartre—and admired leftist protesters who were arrested and tortured. Watching the collapse of the Algerian Islamists during civil war while in exile left a deep impact. According to Azzam S. Tamimi, he was influenced by Malik Bennabi and his treatise "Islam and Democracy," which laid the foundations for Ghannouchi’s "masterpiece" Al‐Hurriyat al‐'Ammah (Public Liberties). In 2002, a Western source (Martin Kramer) described him as differing from other Islamists in his insistence that Islam accepts multi-party democracy. In 2015, he told French journalist Olivier Ravanello that homosexuality should not be criminalized, though he opposed gay marriage; he has also been interviewed by Michael Moore in Where to Invade Next and stated that homosexuality is a "private affair." On 13 July 2021, the official TAP news agency reported that Ghannouchi, already vaccinated, tested positive for COVID-19. On 1 August, he was discharged a few hours after being readmitted to a hospital.
